title: The Sore Weightlifter
briefing: Marcus, 16, did his first real leg workout on Monday. Monday night he felt fine. Wednesday he could barely walk down the stairs. By Saturday the soreness was gone — and the following Monday the same workout felt easier.
question: Why did the pain arrive late, leave slowly, and make him stronger?

clues.title: Fine on Monday night
clues.text: Right after the workout his legs felt tired but not sore. He slept well.
clues.shows: that the soreness is not the workout itself but something that builds afterwards

clues.title: Worst on Wednesday
clues.text: Two days later: stiff, tender to the touch, and stairs are a struggle. Rest makes it ache less, movement warms it up.
clues.shows: soreness peaking about two days after the effort

clues.title: Gone by Saturday
clues.text: Five days on, the soreness has faded completely and his legs feel normal.

clues.title: Easier the next week
clues.text: Same weights, same sets, the following Monday — and it feels noticeably easier, with much less soreness afterwards.
clues.shows: the muscle ending up slightly stronger than before

hypotheses.text: He injured his legs and should not have trained.
hypotheses.flaw: An injury hurts right away and gets worse with use; this arrived two days later, faded on its own, and left him stronger.

hypotheses.text: Hard work made tiny tears in his muscle fibres; the repair process over several days causes the delayed soreness and rebuilds the fibres slightly stronger.
He has a build-up of 'lactic acid' from the workout.
hypotheses.flaw: The burning during exercise clears within about an hour; it cannot explain soreness that starts the next day and peaks two days later.

hypotheses.text: He is just unfit and will always feel this way.
hypotheses.flaw: If nothing changed, the second Monday would feel exactly the same — but it was easier.

prediction.prompt: Starting on workout day and going through the week, how does Marcus's soreness change from day 0 to day 7?

second.question: By the end of the week, how does his strength compare with before the workout?

concepts.label: tiny tears in the fibres
concepts.hint: What did the hard work do to the muscle at a tiny scale?

concepts.label: soreness comes later
concepts.hint: When did the soreness show up, compared with the workout?

concepts.label: repair over days
concepts.hint: What is the body doing during the sore days?

concepts.label: rebuilt stronger
concepts.hint: Why did the second Monday feel different?

concepts.label: rest lets it happen
concepts.hint: What does the repair need that a workout cannot give?

transfer.context: Jade starts a new dance class on Tuesday. On Thursday her calves are too sore to go up on her toes; by the next week's class she manages the whole routine.
options: She pulled a muscle and should quit the class.
New movements made tiny tears in her calf muscles; repairing them caused the delayed soreness and left them a little stronger for next week.
The dance floor was too hard.
Her shoes were the wrong size.
transfer.retryHint: Fine on the day, sore two days later, better the next week — which of Marcus's clues is that pattern?
transfer.explanation: Jade's calves did new work, which tore fibres at a tiny scale. The repair took a few days (the Thursday soreness) and rebuilt them a little stronger — which is why the following week's routine was within reach. Same timeline as Marcus's legs.

takeaway: Muscles get stronger by being repaired. Hard work causes tiny tears; the repair takes days, hurts a little in the middle, and finishes slightly stronger than before — which is why rest days are part of training.
